title: Burst Balloons
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every bursting order directly versus interval DP reasoning about the last balloon burst.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given n balloons with numbers, bursting balloon i earns nums[left] times nums[i] times nums[right] coins, where left and right are the CURRENTLY adjacent balloons at the moment of bursting (using 1 if an index is out of bounds). Return the maximum coins obtainable by bursting all balloons, choosing the order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums array"],["Output","Maximum total coins from bursting all balloons in some order"],["Key Insight","Thinking about which balloon is burst LAST within a range (not first) cleanly splits the range into two independent sub-ranges"],["Constraints","Up to 300 balloons"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Bursting a balloon depends on its CURRENT neighbors, which change as other balloons are removed\"","A classic interval DP problem, best solved by reasoning about which balloon is burst LAST within a range, rather than first"]]}

blocks.text: Thinking about the FIRST balloon to burst in a range is awkward, since the "left" and "right" neighbors used in its coin formula depend on which OTHER balloons still remain, a constantly shifting set. Instead, thinking about which balloon is burst LAST within a range (left, right) is much cleaner: at the moment it is burst, ALL other balloons within (left, right) have already been removed, so its neighbors are GUARANTEED to be exactly the fixed boundary balloons at left and right, regardless of the order everything else was removed in. This cleanly splits the problem into two independent sub-ranges on either side of that last balloon.

blocks.title: Analogy: Deciding Which Wall to Demolish Last When Clearing a Room
blocks.text: Picture clearing a room of internal walls one at a time, where demolishing a wall earns a reward based on its two CURRENTLY adjacent walls at the time. Instead of guessing which wall to knock down first (whose neighbors keep shifting unpredictably), deciding which wall is knocked down LAST is cleaner, since its final neighbors are guaranteed to be the two boundary walls of the room, no matter what order the others were removed in.

blocks.caption: Reason about which balloon is burst LAST within a range, splitting it into two independent sub-ranges

blocks.text: Result: 167 (bursting in the order 1, 5, 3, 8 achieves this maximum).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Pad the array with a 1 on both ends (representing "virtual" boundary balloons that are never actually burst), turning the problem into finding the best way to burst everything STRICTLY BETWEEN two fixed boundary positions.

Observation 2: Define dp[left][right] as the maximum coins obtainable from bursting every balloon strictly between positions left and right (exclusive), where left and right themselves are never burst and remain fixed.

Observation 3: For a given range (left, right), try EVERY possible balloon k strictly between them as the LAST one burst in that range; when it is burst last, its neighbors are guaranteed to be exactly balloons at left and right (everything else in between is already gone), earning balloons[left] times balloons[k] times balloons[right] coins, PLUS whatever was earned bursting everything in (left, k) and everything in (k, right), both independent smaller sub-problems.

Observation 4: dp[left][right] is the MAXIMUM of this quantity over every choice of k, and the final answer is dp[0][n-1] where n is the padded array's length.
This leads to an interval DP over dp[left][right], trying every possible LAST-burst balloon within each range, building from smaller ranges to larger ones.
Conceptually, try every possible ORDER of bursting all balloons directly, computing the total coins for each complete ordering and keeping the best.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every ordering directly implements the definition of "choose the best order" literally.
This costs O(n factorial), utterly infeasible for even moderately sized inputs; reasoning about the LAST balloon burst per range brings this down to a polynomial interval DP instead.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n factorial) to try every ordering.
Space: O(n) per ordering to track current neighbors.
Limitation: reasoning about which balloon is burst LAST (not first) within a range collapses the ordering choice into an interval DP with polynomial states.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Pad nums with a 1 at both ends, forming balloons. Build a 2D DP table dp[left][right], filled by increasing RANGE LENGTH: for every range (left, right) with at least one balloon strictly between them, try every possible k in that open interval as the LAST balloon burst there, computing balloons[left]*balloons[k]*balloons[right] + dp[left][k] + dp[k][right], and take the maximum over all k. The final answer is dp[0][n-1] for the padded array of length n.
Use interval DP, filling ranges by increasing length, trying every possible last-burst balloon within each range.
Dry run intuition for nums = [3,1,5,8] (padded to [1,3,1,5,8,1])

codes.python:
def max_coins(nums):
    balloons = [1] + nums + [1]
    n = len(balloons)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for length in range(2, n):                              # range length, smallest first
        for left in range(n - length):
            right = left + length
            best = 0
            for k in range(left + 1, right):                    # try every LAST-burst balloon
                coins = balloons[left] * balloons[k] * balloons[right] + dp[left][k] + dp[k][right]
                best = max(best, coins)
            dp[left][right] = best
    return dp[0][n - 1]

blocks.text: By reasoning about the LAST balloon burst within a range rather than the first, its neighbors are GUARANTEED to be the fixed boundary balloons at left and right, since everything else strictly between them has already been removed by that point, regardless of the specific order used to remove them; this correctly and cleanly splits the problem into two fully independent smaller sub-ranges, avoiding ever needing to track a constantly shifting set of "current neighbors" directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), trying every range and every possible last-burst position within it.
Space: O(n squared) for the DP table.

blocks.text: Burst Balloons is the canonical "think backward, about what happens LAST" interval DP problem: reversing the natural forward framing is the key unlock.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "an item's value depends on its CURRENT neighbors, which shift as other items are removed", think: interval DP reasoning about what happens LAST, not first.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force ordering search costs O(n factorial), utterly infeasible; the interval DP costs O(n cubed), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: interval dynamic programming, reasoning about what happens LAST within a range rather than first.
Core Idea: pad with virtual boundary balloons; dp[left][right] tries every possible last-burst balloon, combining two independent sub-ranges.
Time: O(n factorial) for the brute force, O(n cubed) for the interval DP.
Space: O(n) per ordering for the brute force, O(n squared) for the interval DP.
Most Important Observation: the LAST balloon burst in a range has guaranteed, fixed neighbors, unlike the first.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, classic interval DP problem with a clever reframing trick.
One line memory trick: think about what is destroyed last, not first.
